name: satnaing.dev
object_type: Portfolio — a conventional personal portfolio-plus-blog for a working full-stack developer. It is the most 'textbook' item in the benchmark set: a single-page marketing homepage (hero / about / projects / blog teaser / contact) bolted to a multi-page Markdown blog. Secondarily it functions as a template/OSS artifact, because the site's own source is public and has been forked 51 times, so other developers use it as a starting point.
format_genre: Scroll-page. The homepage is one long vertical scroll with four anchored sections (#whoami, #projects, #blog, #contact) plus a hero, and a scroll-spy indicator that highlights the active section. The blog is a separate conventional multi-page document area (/blog, /blog/categories, /blog/tags, /blog/posts/<slug>). Notably, the owner also runs a second site in a completely different genre — terminal.satnaing.dev, a terminal-CLI portfolio — and lists it on this site as a project rather than merging the two. So the genre choice here is deliberate: the mainstream scroll-page is the 'front door', the terminal experiment is content inside it.
intent_audience: Mixed job-seeking + freelance client acquisition, with a growing personal-brand/authority layer. On-site the CTA is employment-and-collaboration flavoured and deliberately non-specific: 'As a dev, I am driven by my love for coding and my desire for new challenges. If you have opportunities for collaboration or want to build something amazing, don't hesitate to contact me!' → a single 'Get in touch!' mailto button. The freelance intent is stated off-site rather than on-site (his GitHub profile README says 'I'm available for freelance projects. You can reach me at contact@satnaing.dev' and links GitHub Sponsors). The authority layer is implicit and undersold: his open-source work (AstroPaper ~4.9k stars, shadcn-admin ~12.8k stars) is by far his strongest credential, but the site frames those as 'Featured Projects' rather than as a body of influential OSS work. There is no gated qualification, no intake form, no availability status, no rate card.
seniority_stage: Mid-level, as presented. The site self-describes as 'a Full-Stack Developer' with '4+ years of comprehensive experience', leads with education rather than employment, and lists no job titles or employers at all. External sources put him further along than the site does: his GitHub profile lists Senior Frontend Developer at Trienpont International and the profile company field now reads 'Onify Tech' with location Bangkok, Thailand, while LinkedIn surfaces as 'Senior Software Engineer | Frontend Expert' [uncertain]. 'Good' for this item therefore means legibility and craft — a recruiter or client should be able to grasp skills, evidence and contact route in one scroll — and by that standard the site succeeds. Its stage-mismatch is the interesting failure: the seniority signals have outgrown the page.
language_i18n: Interface is English only — `<html lang="en">`, all nav/UI/section copy in English, no language switcher for the site chrome. There is, however, real content-level bilingualism in the blog: a 'Blog Posts Language:' filter with All / English / Myanmar, and one post is written entirely in Burmese ('Haru Fashion ecommerce ကိုဘယ်လိုရေးခဲ့လဲ'). One project (Haru Fashion) is itself described as 'Available in English and Burmese languages'. No EN/RU toggle. The pattern worth noting for the RU cohort: he kept a single English UI and treated the second language as a content dimension with a filter, rather than duplicating the whole site.
owner_role: Sat Naing — self-described 'Full-Stack Developer' and 'Passionate Programmer / Freelancer', stated on the site as based in Yangon, Myanmar. Claims React and Next.js on the frontend, and PHP, CodeIgniter, Node.js and Express on the backend. Education-forward: B.Sc (Hons) Computing, Edinburgh Napier University (2018–2019, First Class Honours, merit in 7 of 9 modules); HND Computing & System Development, Info Myanmar University (2016–2018, overall Merit); IELTS 6.5, British Council Myanmar (2017). Off-site he is a notable open-source author (AstroPaper, shadcn-admin, terminal-portfolio) with ~1.17k GitHub followers, currently a senior frontend engineer and now based in Bangkok, Thailand — none of which the site reflects.
sections_present: PRESENT: About (labelled 'Who am I?'), Projects ('Featured Projects', 6 cards), Blog (carousel of 4 recent posts on the homepage plus a full blog area at /blog with categories and tags indexes), Contact (headline + paragraph + single mailto button). ABSENT and conspicuously so: Experience / work history — there is no employment timeline, no employer names, no job titles anywhere on the site; the About section's content is education instead. Also absent: a Skills section (skills appear only as per-project tech tags and one sentence in the hero), Resume/CV in any form (/resume, /cv, /resume.pdf all 404), Testimonials, Services/pricing, Now/status page, Uses page. Blog sub-structure is more developed than the portfolio side: category index, tag index, English/Myanmar language filter, featured-vs-all post split, and a client-side search box per the repo README.
nav_pattern: Hybrid. The homepage is single-page anchor scroll; the blog is genuinely multi-page. Chrome: a fixed top bar with a glassmorphism backdrop carrying the 'SatNaing.dev' wordmark, four section links, and a light/dark toggle button (`title="Toggles light & dark theme"`, `aria-live="polite"`). On mobile the same nav relocates to a fixed bottom pill bar with icon-above-label items — an app-style tab bar rather than a hamburger, which is the single best structural idea on the site. On desktop there is additionally a left-edge scroll-spy rail of four small rotated-square dots with `title` tooltips (Welcome / Who am i? / Projects / Contact), driven by a `useScrollActive` hook. The blog area swaps in its own nav (Home / Categories / Tags / Portfolio / contact@satnaing.dev). A real skip link ('Skip to main content' → #main) is the first focusable element and is translate-hidden until focused.
visual_style: Clean, warm, illustration-led minimalism with a distinctly 2021–2022 vintage. The hero pairs a hand-drawn character illustration of the owner (commissioned from a friend and credited in the repo README — a nice attribution norm) with a laptop illustration and rotating role labels (PASSIONATE PROGRAMMER / FREELANCER / FULL-STACK DEVELOPER). Decorative dotted-grid SVG accents sit behind the About section with separate light and dark variants. Cards are soft-cornered with a per-project pastel background colour behind each 16:9 screenshot, and images scale on hover. Design-trend alignment: it is squarely minimal + a light touch of glassmorphism — the nav bar and the mobile tab bar are explicitly `glassmorphism` / `lower-glassmorphism` classes with backdrop blur (added in v2.2.0 per the changelog). It is NOT bento grid, NOT neo-brutalist, NOT kinetic typography, and it makes no attempt at the 2025–2026 trend cycle. The dominant impression is competent, friendly and safe — it looks like a well-executed 2022 Next.js portfolio, because that is exactly when it was built. The repo README openly names its design references: Lee Robinson's site, the PaperMod Hugo theme, Brittany Chiang's site, and mxb.dev — i.e. two other members of this very benchmark set.
color_typography: Single-accent teal/green system with paired light and dark accents so contrast holds in both modes: light mode uses 'marrsgreen' #007A7A (hover #1C9A9A, active #004D4D) on background #F9FAFB with #EFF3F3 cards; dark mode uses 'carrigreen' #05CE91 (hover #57DCB4, active #00835B) on background #1D2A35 with #22323F cards and #F9FAFB text. `theme-color` is #1D2A35. Typography is a single family — Jost (geometric sans, Google Fonts, weights 400/500/600/700 + 400 italic), loaded with `display=swap` and inlined @font-face by Next.js, with `preconnect` to fonts.gstatic.com. Dark mode is a real class-based implementation (`darkMode: "class"` in Tailwind config + `next-themes`) with an explicit user toggle in the header AND system-preference default — the strongest dark-mode implementation in this set, and better than leerob.com, which is system-only with no toggle.
motion: Moderate and GSAP-driven (GSAP 3.11; the changelog records replacing Framer Motion with GSAP in v2.0.0). Effects: a page loader on first paint; per-section reveal/wipe animations tied to a `useOnScreen` hook (headings and education blocks animate out of `overflow-hidden` wrappers); rotating hero role text; hover scale on project images and a hover-rotate on the GitHub/star icons; a Swiper carousel with prev/next/pagination for blog cards; and a global custom cursor — a `mousemove` listener in `_app` that GSAP-tweens a follower element's x/y, fading it out on `mouseleave`/`mousedown`. `prefers-reduced-motion` is NOT respected: the string appears zero times in either shipped CSS file, and there is no reduced-motion branch in the JS. Given the README's 'Fully Accessible ♿️' claim, this is the clearest gap between claim and implementation on the site.
responsiveness_mobile: Genuinely responsive and, for its genre, better than average — because the format_genre degrades gracefully by design rather than by luck. Tailwind breakpoints are custom: xs 480, sm 640, md 768, lg 976, xl 1440. The scroll-page format has no inherent mobile penalty, and the one structural risk (a top nav with four links plus a theme toggle) is solved properly: below md the nav detaches from the header and becomes a fixed bottom glassmorphism tab bar with 24px icons above short labels, each item a fixed 4.5rem wide — thumb-reachable and unmistakably native-feeling. Other mobile-aware choices: project cards go from two-up (`md:basis-1/2`) to one-up; the desktop-only left scroll-spy rail is `hidden md:flex` so it never crowds a phone; decorative dotted SVGs are `hidden lg:inline-block` so mobile never downloads or renders them; images ship as WebP through next/image with a full srcSet and `loading="lazy"` below the fold, and the two hero images are preloaded with `fetchpriority="high"`. Costs on mobile: the custom GSAP cursor is meaningless on touch and is pure wasted JS there; the Swiper blog carousel is a horizontal-swipe pattern that hides three of four posts behind a gesture; and the bottom tab bar overlays content, so the last few pixels of a section can sit under it.
framework_hosting: Next.js 13.5.6 on the legacy **pages** router (confirmed by `next-head-count`, `_app`/`pages/index` chunks and `__NEXT_DATA__`), React 18.2, TypeScript 4.9.5, Tailwind CSS 3.2 with @tailwindcss/typography and the (now-deprecated) @tailwindcss/line-clamp plugin, `next-themes` 0.2 for dark mode, GSAP 3.11 for animation, Swiper 8.4 for carousels, react-rough-notation 1.0 for hand-drawn annotation marks, and gray-matter + remark/remark-html for Markdown content. Content authoring: Markdown files in a `contents/` directory, historically edited through **Forestry headless CMS** (a `.forestry/` config directory is still in the repo). Forestry was sunset in April 2023, which is almost certainly the mechanical reason the blog stopped — the publishing pipeline died and was never replaced [uncertain]. Hosting has migrated: the README still says Vercel, but the live response headers say `server: Netlify` with `x-nf-render-mode: ssr`, `x-nextjs-cache: HIT` and Netlify Durable/Edge cache-status, and `@netlify/plugin-nextjs` 4.30 is in devDependencies — so it is Netlify SSR/ISR today, on a `.dev` TLD matching the owner's handle (satnaing.dev), with the terminal variant on a subdomain (terminal.satnaing.dev). Design was done in Figma per the README.
performance_a11y: Performance: light-to-moderate and clearly cared about, but dated. Homepage HTML is ~80 KB uncompressed (SSR, content in the markup); the two CSS files are 55 KB + 12 KB uncompressed; JS totals roughly 680 KB uncompressed across 11 chunks (framework 141 KB, main 98 KB, _app 75 KB, a 102 KB vendor chunk, a 91 KB polyfills chunk that a modern-only build would not need, and a tiny 261-byte page chunk). Images are all WebP via next/image with correct srcSets and lazy-loading, so the render path is fast; TTFB measured ~0.5 s from Netlify's edge with an SSR cache hit. The repo README embeds a Lighthouse-score SVG linked to a live PageSpeed report, so performance was explicitly tracked at build time [uncertain whether current scores still match]. Accessibility: better than most portfolios and deliberately worked on — a genuine skip link as the first focusable element (`SkipToMain.tsx`), `focus-visible` outline utilities applied consistently to links and buttons (`link-outline`, `focus-visible:outline-marrsgreen`), `role="list"` on styled lists, an `sr-only` span supplying the ' at ' text between date and time on blog cards, decorative SVGs correctly marked `aria-hidden="true"` (21 instances), meaningful `alt` text on every content image including the illustrations, the theme toggle marked `aria-live="polite"`, and a paired light/dark accent palette chosen for contrast. Gaps: `prefers-reduced-motion` is not honoured anywhere; blog post dates are rendered client-side (`DateTime.tsx`), so the server HTML shows 'Posted on: | at' with no date at all — bad for crawlers and for no-JS readers; the per-project stargazer link renders in SSR with a `title` but no `href`, so it is a non-functional control until hydration; and there is no `<noscript>` fallback. robots.txt and sitemap.xml both exist and return 200. The README's blanket 'Fully Accessible ♿️' claim overstates it, but the effort behind the claim is real.
analytics_instrumentation: Google Analytics 4 only — measurement ID G-R824JTDVDJ, injected via `next/script` with `strategy="lazyOnload"` in `_app`, so it does not block the render path. No Plausible, Umami, Fathom, Vercel Analytics, PostHog or session-replay tooling; nothing appears in the initial HTML head. There is no cookie/consent banner.
project_presentation:
Six curated cards in a two-column flex grid under the heading 'Featured Projects' and a self-aware subhead — '“Talk is cheap. Show me the code”? I got you. Here are some of my projects you shouldn't misss' (the typo 'misss' is live). Each card carries: a 16:9 WebP screenshot on a per-project pastel background, the project title, a one- or two-sentence description, a flat list of tech tags, and a row of three actions — a **live GitHub stargazer count** (a `githubApi` URL per project, e.g. `https://api.github.com/repos/satnaing/astro-paper`, fetched client-side and shown next to a star glyph, added in a Feb 2024 commit), a GitHub repo link, and a live-demo link. There is also a per-project `type` field in the source ('Frontend', 'Backend', 'Frontend + HeadlessCMS').

The six: (1) AstroPaper — Astro blog theme, described as 'One of the most starred blog templates built with Astro'; demo astro-paper.pages.dev (Cloudflare Pages), repo satnaing/astro-paper (~4.9k stars, MIT). (2) Terminal Portfolio — demo terminal.satnaing.dev (own subdomain), repo satnaing/terminal-portfolio (~795 stars, MIT). (3) Haru Fashion — ecommerce SPA, demo haru-fashion.vercel.app (Vercel), repo satnaing/haru-fashion. (4) Haru API — REST API for Haru, 'demo' is the API docs at satnaing.github.io/haru-api (GitHub Pages), repo satnaing/haru-api. (5) Next Bookstore — Next.js 13 appDir + Strapi CMS, demo nextbookstore.vercel.app (Vercel), repo satnaing/next-bookstore. (6) Shadcn Admin — admin dashboard UI, 'Built with responsiveness and accessibility in mind', demo shadcn-admin.netlify.app (Netlify), repo satnaing/shadcn-admin (~12.8k stars, MIT).

Live-demo availability is effectively 100% and the hosting spread is itself informative: Cloudflare Pages, own subdomain, Vercel ×2, GitHub Pages, Netlify — free-tier hosts chosen per project rather than one platform. Below the grid, a single honest overflow link: 'Other projects can be explored in my github profile'.

What is missing: no per-project case-study page, no problem/approach/outcome narrative, no dates, no role/team attribution, no 'what was hard' section, and no filtering or tiering — a 4.9k-star OSS theme and a personal ecommerce practice project sit on the same visual footing. The star counter is the single strongest idea here (it converts 'I built this' into a live third-party number without any manual maintenance), but it is rendered as a bare glyph without a label, so a visitor may not realise what the number means.
resume_integration_mode: None of the four modes. No PDF download, no inline HTML CV, nothing ATS-parseable, and no /resume or /cv route (all 404). The functional substitute is the About section's education list — degree, institution, years, honours, module counts, IELTS band — which is the one part of the site that reads like a CV. Because employment history is entirely absent from the site, an ATS or a recruiter's parser fed this URL would extract a name, a role label, six project names, a tech-tag soup and three educational credentials, but zero work experience. LinkedIn carries the machine-readable career record. For a mid-to-senior engineer this is the site's largest structural omission.
proof_verifiability: Strong on code, weak on career. What IS verifiable and well-linked: every project has both a public GitHub repo link and a working live demo, so 'I built this' is checkable in one click; the live stargazer count per project is pulled straight from the GitHub API, meaning the popularity claim is a third-party number the owner cannot fudge; the site's OWN source code is public, so the portfolio verifies itself; the repo README embeds a Lighthouse-score badge linking to a live PageSpeed report; and the README explicitly credits the design references it borrowed from and states 'I can guarantee that I wrote 100% of the code', while separately crediting the friend who drew the hero illustration — unusually good attribution hygiene. What is NOT verifiable: the '4+ years of comprehensive experience' claim has nothing behind it (no employers, no dates, no references); the AstroPaper claim 'One of the most starred blog templates built with Astro' is plausible and roughly true at ~4.9k stars but is not linked to any ranking; and the academic honours (First Class, 'merit in 7 modules out of 9', IELTS 6.5) are stated without any certificate, transcript or issuer link. Net: the engineering claims are near-self-verifying, the biographical claims rest entirely on trust.
quantified_impact: Almost none in the conventional sense — and this is a real missed opportunity, because the numbers exist. The site's only on-page metrics are the live per-project GitHub star counts and the education figures ('7 modules out of 9', 'band score 6.5', '4+ years'). There are no user counts, no traffic figures, no latency/accuracy/uptime numbers, no revenue or cost-saved claims, no 'reduced X by Y%' — nothing framed in outcome terms. Meanwhile the owner's actual verifiable impact is substantial and sits just off-page: shadcn-admin at ~12.8k stars and ~2.0k forks, AstroPaper at ~4.9k stars and ~1.04k forks, terminal-portfolio at ~795 stars and ~159 forks, and this portfolio repo itself at ~174 stars and 51 forks, plus ~1.17k GitHub followers. The site surfaces the star numbers as an unlabelled glyph and never aggregates them, never says 'my open-source work has been forked 3,000+ times', and never connects any project to a downstream user or client. The contrast with the RU cohort is instructive: this owner has the strongest hard numbers of any mid-level developer in the set and displays them the most quietly.
content_freshness:
This is the site's weakest dimension and the most useful lesson in it. The site is live, fast and perfectly maintained-looking, but it has been frozen for roughly two and a half years. Evidence: the public repo's last commit on the default branch is 2024-02-14 ('✨ Add github stars in project', '📝 Update about section') with a last push of 2024-05-10; the blog's newest post is dated 2022-06-09 and there are only four posts total; the framework is Next.js 13 pages-router in an era of Next.js 16 app-router; the authoring CMS (Forestry) has been dead since April 2023. There is no 'currently working on', no now-page, no last-updated stamp, no RSS-driven recency signal.

Three visible staleness tells a careful visitor will catch: (1) a placeholder post titled 'This is just a testing' with lorem-ipsum body text, dated 2020-06-17, is published and appears in the homepage blog carousel AND in the /blog 'All Posts' list — a test record left in production for years; (2) the typo 'misss' in the Projects subhead; (3) the biography is factually out of date — the site says 'based in Yangon, Myanmar' with '4+ years of experience' and no employer, while his GitHub profile now reads Bangkok, Thailand and a senior role. The site is not abandoned in the sense of broken — every link and demo still works, and the linked projects themselves (astro-paper, shadcn-admin) are actively maintained as recently as 2026-07-21. The freshness lives in the repos; the shop window has not been dusted.
writing_tone: Warm, earnest, slightly formal-ESL, first person, and modestly self-promotional without swagger. Hero: 'Hi my name is Sat Naing, A Full-stack Developer… I am a Full-Stack Developer with a passion for delivering exceptional results.' It leans on stock professional phrasing ('exceptional results', 'unique combination of technical skills and creative problem-solving', 'polished my skills') that reads as competent-but-generic. Two flashes of genuine personality: the projects subhead quotes Linus Torvalds — '“Talk is cheap. Show me the code”? I got you.' — and the contact headline is 'Let's be awesome together!'. The blog framing is refreshingly honest about motive: 'I write blog posts about what I've done and what I'm doing as a documenting practice', and the blog intro promises 'my projects (what I do/how I did), my personal experiences, and some random stuffs'. Footer signs off 'Coded with love by Sat Naing'. Contrast worth noting for the report: leerob.com's copy is shorter, plainer and more confident precisely because it makes fewer adjectival claims; this site's tone is the standard mid-career portfolio register, and its two Torvalds-quote / 'let's be awesome' moments are the parts that actually stick.
standout_features:
Ranked by borrowability for a comparable mid-level SE portfolio on a small time budget.

CHEAP AND WORTH STEALING:
1. **Live GitHub stargazer count per project card**, driven by a `githubApi` field in the project data array and fetched client-side. This is the single best idea on the site: it converts a subjective 'featured project' into a third-party number that updates itself forever with zero maintenance. Improve on it by adding a visible label ('★ 4.9k on GitHub') instead of a bare glyph, and by rendering the count server-side so it survives no-JS and crawlers.
2. **Every project gets BOTH a repo link and a working live demo**, with the demo host chosen per project (Cloudflare Pages, Vercel, GitHub Pages, Netlify, own subdomain). Six for six, no dead links, no screenshot-only entries.
3. **Mobile nav as a fixed bottom glassmorphism tab bar** with icon-above-label items, replacing the desktop top nav below `md`. Costs a handful of Tailwind responsive classes and instantly makes the phone experience feel app-native instead of hamburger-generic.
4. **Real skip link as a dedicated component** (`SkipToMain.tsx`) plus consistent `focus-visible` outline utilities and correct `aria-hidden` on all 21 decorative SVGs. Cheap, and the only reason the site can plausibly market itself as accessible.
5. **Paired light/dark accent colours** (#007A7A light / #05CE91 dark) rather than one accent forced through both themes — the reason contrast holds in both modes. A five-minute decision most portfolios get wrong.
6. **Dark mode with a real user toggle plus system default** (`next-themes` + Tailwind `darkMode: 'class'`), announced with `aria-live="polite"`. Stronger than leerob.com, which is system-preference-only.
7. **A content-language filter instead of a duplicated site** — one English UI, a per-post language field, and an All/English/Myanmar toggle on the blog index. The cheapest credible answer to bilingual content, and directly applicable to an EN/RU requirement.
8. **A commissioned character illustration of the owner** (drawn by a friend, credited in the repo) as the hero visual. It differentiates instantly from the sea of headshot-or-nothing portfolios at the cost of one favour or one small commission.
9. **Publishing the site's own source with a documented tech-stack table, a Lighthouse badge linking to a live PageSpeed report, a CHANGELOG, and an explicit 'Inspiration and Credits' section naming the sites it learned from.** The credits section in particular is a strong authenticity signal and costs four bullet points.
10. **A CHANGELOG.md for a personal website**, with semver releases (v1.0.0 → v2.3.0) and emoji-prefixed commits. Turns maintenance into a visible artifact.

MEDIUM COST:
11. **A second site in a completely different genre** (terminal.satnaing.dev) treated as a project ON the main site. This is the cleanest resolution of the 'should my portfolio be gimmicky or legible?' dilemma anywhere in this research set: make the legible one the front door and ship the gimmick as evidence. It also earned 795 stars, so the gimmick paid for itself.
12. Blog with category index, tag index, featured/all split and client-side search — a genuinely structured content area rather than a bolted-on list.

ANTI-PATTERNS TO AVOID (this site demonstrates all four):
13. **No Experience section and no resume of any kind.** For a mid-to-senior engineer this is the biggest single omission; it forces every serious evaluator off-site to LinkedIn.
14. **A published lorem-ipsum test post ('This is just a testing') sitting in production for years**, surfacing in both the homepage carousel and the blog index. One five-minute deletion would remove the strongest 'this site is unmaintained' signal on the page.
15. **Letting the bio go stale** — wrong city, understated experience, no employer — while the linked repos stay actively maintained. Freshness in the repos does not transfer to the shop window.
16. **Marketing 'Fully Accessible ♿️' while shipping zero `prefers-reduced-motion` handling** and client-only rendered dates. If you claim it, honour it.
originality_vs_template: Custom build, no template lineage — and it has become a template lineage of its own. The README states plainly: 'Here are some inspiration and credits for the design of my portfolio. However I can guarantee that I wrote 100% of the code. These credits are just for ideas and design' — then names four references, two of which are in this benchmark set: leerob.io (Lee Robinson), Brittany Chiang, the PaperMod Hugo theme, and mxb.dev (Max Böck). The hero illustration is explicitly credited to a friend (Swann Fevian Kyaw / @ToonHa). The code itself is hand-written Next.js with bespoke components (`ProjectCard`, `EduGroup`, `SkipToMain`, `useOnScreen`, `useScrollActive`) and no starter-kit fingerprints. Downstream, the repo has ~174 stars and 51 forks, so it is now itself a source template — and its author is separately one of the most-forked portfolio/theme authors on GitHub via astro-paper (~1.04k forks) and shadcn-admin (~2.0k forks). Note the absence of a LICENSE file on the portfolio repo, which technically makes those 51 forks legally unlicensed.
source_available: Yes — github.com/satnaing/satnaing.dev, ~174 stars, 51 forks, created 2022-03-14, last pushed 2024-05-10, **no license file** (all rights reserved by default, despite being visibly forked 51 times). The repo is unusually well-documented for a personal site: a README with a screenshot, tech-stack table, a Lighthouse-score SVG linked to a live PageSpeed report, local-setup instructions, an explicit credits/inspiration section, and a separate CHANGELOG.md tracking v1.0.0 (2022-03-24) through v2.3.0. Content lives as Markdown in `contents/`, with a `.forestry/` CMS config still committed. This is a strong dogfooding signal — the site, its source, and its documentation are all part of the same portfolio argument — and it is reinforced by the fact that four of the six featured projects are themselves public MIT repos. The one gap is the missing licence.
contact_methods: Deliberately minimal and single-channel. The Contact section offers exactly one action: a 'Get in touch!' button linking to `mailto:contact@satnaing.dev` (with `target="_self"`). No contact form, no Calendly, no newsletter capture, no phone. Social links are placed in the footer via a `SocialLinks` component and in the blog nav: GitHub (github.com/satnaing), LinkedIn (linkedin.com/in/satnaing), dev.to (dev.to/satnaing), and Facebook (facebook.com/satnaing.dev) — the Facebook inclusion is a regional norm signal (Myanmar/SEA) that would read as unusual on a Western portfolio. The blog header additionally shows the email address as visible text. Notably absent from the site despite being on his GitHub profile: X/Twitter, Instagram, CodePen, and GitHub Sponsors. LinkedIn is present but there is no CV to pair with it.
pii_exposure: Low and well-managed. The email exposed is a role-style address on his own domain (contact@satnaing.dev), not a personal Gmail — the correct pattern, and shown both as a mailto and as visible text in the blog header. Real name and city are public by intent, though the stated city (Yangon, Myanmar) is now out of date relative to his GitHub profile (Bangkok, Thailand), which is arguably a privacy benefit by accident. A real profile photograph is present alongside the commissioned illustration. No phone number, no postal address, no date of birth, no employer-internal detail, and no scanned certificates despite the academic claims. Visitor-side: Google Analytics 4 runs with no cookie or consent banner, and the client-side stargazer fetches hit api.github.com directly from the visitor's browser, which discloses the visitor's IP to GitHub on every page view — a minor third-party leak most implementations of this pattern share.
